items.title: The Witcher 3 and Assassin's Creed 'Reset Player Expectations' for Open-World Action RPGs, So the Fable Reboot Devs Had to Look Beyond the Original Trilogy for Inspiration
items.description: Why has the Fable reboot taken so long to develop? There are a number of reasons, but part of it is that expectations around open-world action RPGs were reset by various competing games over the past decade.
items.author: Wesley Yin-Poole
items.content:
Why has the Fable reboot taken so long to develop? There are a number of reasons, but part of it is that expectations around open-world action RPGs were reset by various competing games over the past decade.

Work on Fable reportedly started in 2016, and only now, 10 years later, is it near release. It’s suffered a tumultuous development but, unlike some other costly Microsoft gaming projects, it has avoided closure amid sweeping layoffs and restructuring at Xbox.

In a new interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Playground Games co-founder and Fable general manager Ralph Fulton touched on the trials and tribulations Fable has endured over the years. Playground set up a new team to make Fable in addition to its hugely popular racing game franchise, Forza Horizon, and set out to make a game in a genre it had no prior experience with. And Fable is a big role-playing game, with all the bells and whistles you'd expect. So, Fable isn’t technically a debut game from Playground, but it sort of is.

In terms of what’s changed, Fulton said that technology had “advanced” during development, pointing to a reset of player expectations with the release of CD Projekt’s fantasy RPG masterpiece The Witcher 3 and then Assassin’s Creed’s move towards the RPG genre.

This, Fulton explained, meant that Playground had to look beyond the original Fable trilogy for inspiration to ensure it created a reboot that would meet modern open-world standards.

“In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard,” Fulton explained. “And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG.

“All of these games continue to reset player expectations, which means I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects.”

Despite this, the scope of Fable actually decreased over time, with the project starting with “an enormous potential scope.” In August, Playground confirmed that Fable’s main quest will take around 20 hours to beat, with an additional 15-20 hours of side and open-world exploration content available. Howlongtobeat has the original 2004 Fable's main quest clocking in at about 12-and-a-half hours. Fable 2 isn't much longer at 13 hours, and Fable 3 inches just further past that at 13-and-a-half hours. So, the Fable reboot is shaping up to be the longest in the series.

Fable is set for launch on February 23, 2027, across PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S.

items.title: Blade Runner 2099 Showrunner Explains the References to Philip K. Dick's Novel, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
items.description: Silka Luisa, the creator, executive producer, and showrunner of Blade Runner 2099, explained why this series was the first entry in the franchise to include certain references from Philip K. Dick’s original novel.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Silka Luisa, the creator, executive producer, and showrunner of Blade Runner 2099, recently explained to IGN why this series was the first entry in the franchise to include certain references to Philip K. Dick’s original novel.

Warning: MAJOR spoilers for Blade Runner 2099 ahead! Turn back now if you haven’t watched the show!

Philip K. Dick’s genre-defining sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is the basis upon which Ridley Scott built the first Blade Runner movie back in 1982. It certainly had its differences from the source material — though Dick himself praised a television preview he saw just before his death — and was notably lacking a few central elements from the book, chief among them the empathy box and Deckard’s hand-wringing over a vanity purchase of an actual, real-life animal (hence the book’s title).

Near the beginning of the book, Deckard is in knots about keeping up with the Joneses; in the novel’s post-war future where global conditions have been extremely averse to almost all forms of life, animals are a rarity, and owning one is a luxury. Deckard and his wife — to whom he appears to harbor relative indifference, if not annoyance — own an electric sheep, which they keep on the rooftop of their apartment building.

Unable to stand the constraints of his financial class, he decides to purchase a black Nubian goat, which he hesitantly shows to his wife, who predictably blows up at him for making such a massive purchase without consulting her. She eventually comes around to the animal after actually setting eyes on it, however. (Eventually, the goat is killed by Rachael, a replicant with whom Deckard has an affair.) While this specific storyline isn’t in the original movie nor any subsequent Blade Runner media, a black goat does appear in Silka’s show.

This goat makes its appearance on the sea cliffs near Cora and Elias’s childhood home, which is where they lived with their adoptive mother, Helena. As Cora later comes to discover, Helena was one of the very first replicants ever made, a Nexus 1, created without a set lifespan and essentially immortal (as long as they can void injury or accidents). It’s a lovely parallel with the book as the goat represented Deckard’s desperation to cling to his humanity and his status in society. Helena was also a way for Cora to cling to her own humanity in a world run by replicants. But after learning that her mother was a Nexus 1, this illusion crashes down on her, much like the goat after it was pushed off the roof of Deckard’s apartment building by his scorned replicant lover.

Also included for the first time is the empathy box, a technological marvel that allows users to mentally and physically "feel" the events of whatever they are seeing on a screen in front of them. In this case, it’s Wilbur Mercer, a religious figure whose laborious climb up a mountain while being pelted with rocks has become a central part of a religion aptly named "Mercerism." In the book, the footage is discovered to be fake, having been filmed on a sound stage; Mercer was merely a character played by an actor named Al Jarry.

The empathy box shows up in one of the final episodes of Blade Runner 2099. A Mercerite forces the dying replicant Olwen to use the box, where she watches Mercer climb the mountain and feels herself being pelted with stones.

I asked Silka about these references and why she felt they were important to include in the show when previous adaptations had largely ignored them in favor of building upon Scott’s specific version of Dick’s literary world.

“I mean, Philip K. Dick is a genius,” Silka told me. “His book is so prescient. I think what's so special about him and his writing is not just that he was able to look into the future and really see not only what would happen, but the dangers of what would happen, but he also has a way of doing it where it's this playful, zany tone that you almost... It doesn't leave you with a feeling of dread, but the ideas are very, very dark. And the juxtaposition of those two things, this playful tone plus these dark ideas, that felt like a direction and a north star, tonally, for us to pursue.

“And also just as a lover of the book, I love Mercerism. I was so curious as to, ‘Okay, what would an empathy box look like? Who were the practitioners? What did Wilbur's climb actually look like?’ So much of that had lived in my imagination. And so then, to be able to actually sit with people and say, ‘Well, what do you think it looks like?’ And then look at references and build that out, it was really exciting."

Silka Luisa, the creator, executive producer, and showrunner of Blade Runner 2099, recently explained to IGN why this series was the first entry in the franchise to include certain references to Philip K. Dick’s original novel.

Warning: MAJOR spoilers for Blade Runner 2099 ahead! Turn back now if you haven’t watched the show!

Philip K. Dick’s genre-defining sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is the basis upon which Ridley Scott built the first Blade Runner movie back in 1982. It certainly had its differences from the source material — though Dick himself praised a television preview he saw just before his death — and was notably lacking a few central elements from the book, chief among them the empathy box and Deckard’s hand-wringing over a vanity purchase of an actual, real-life animal (hence the book’s title).

Near the beginning of the book, Deckard is in knots about keeping up with the Joneses; in the novel’s post-war future where global conditions have been extremely averse to almost all forms of life, animals are a rarity, and owning one is a luxury. Deckard and his wife — to whom he appears to harbor relative indifference, if not annoyance — own an electric sheep, which they keep on the rooftop of their apartment building.

Unable to stand the constraints of his financial class, he decides to purchase a black Nubian goat, which he hesitantly shows to his wife, who predictably blows up at him for making such a massive purchase without consulting her. She eventually comes around to the animal after actually setting eyes on it, however. (Eventually, the goat is killed by Rachael, a replicant with whom Deckard has an affair.) While this specific storyline isn’t in the original movie nor any subsequent Blade Runner media, a black goat does appear in Silka’s show.

This goat makes its appearance on the sea cliffs near Cora and Elias’s childhood home, which is where they lived with their adoptive mother, Helena. As Cora later comes to discover, Helena was one of the very first replicants ever made, a Nexus 1, created without a set lifespan and essentially immortal (as long as they can void injury or accidents). It’s a lovely parallel with the book as the goat represented Deckard’s desperation to cling to his humanity and his status in society. Helena was also a way for Cora to cling to her own humanity in a world run by replicants. But after learning that her mother was a Nexus 1, this illusion crashes down on her, much like the goat after it was pushed off the roof of Deckard’s apartment building by his scorned replicant lover.

Also included for the first time is the empathy box, a technological marvel that allows users to mentally and physically "feel" the events of whatever they are seeing on a screen in front of them. In this case, it’s Wilbur Mercer, a religious figure whose laborious climb up a mountain while being pelted with rocks has become a central part of a religion aptly named "Mercerism." In the book, the footage is discovered to be fake, having been filmed on a sound stage; Mercer was merely a character played by an actor named Al Jarry.

The empathy box shows up in one of the final episodes of Blade Runner 2099. A Mercerite forces the dying replicant Olwen to use the box, where she watches Mercer climb the mountain and feels herself being pelted with stones.

I asked Silka about these references and why she felt they were important to include in the show when previous adaptations had largely ignored them in favor of building upon Scott’s specific version of Dick’s literary world.

“I mean, Philip K. Dick is a genius,” Silka told me. “His book is so prescient. I think what's so special about him and his writing is not just that he was able to look into the future and really see not only what would happen, but the dangers of what would happen, but he also has a way of doing it where it's this playful, zany tone that you almost... It doesn't leave you with a feeling of dread, but the ideas are very, very dark. And the juxtaposition of those two things, this playful tone plus these dark ideas, that felt like a direction and a north star, tonally, for us to pursue.

“And also just as a lover of the book, I love Mercerism. I was so curious as to, ‘Okay, what would an empathy box look like? Who were the practitioners?
